newsitem.title: UK: UK sleaze row spirals, dogging Major's campaign.
newsitem.headline: UK sleaze row spirals, dogging Major's campaign.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major on Friday denied fresh newspaper allegations about sleaze within his Conservative Party but the bitter row over cash-for-questions deepened the gloom cast by low opinion poll ratings.

Major described as "total junk" allegations that he allowed ruling party MP Tim Smith to continue as junior Northern Ireland minister in 1994 after he was told of charges that Smith took money to ask questions for businessmen in parliament.

But the opposition Labour party drove home its advantage, demanding publication of a report into the influence-peddling before the May 1 election and accusing Major of trying to avoid embarrassment with a cover-up.
"The real scandal is not that the Tory (Conservative) party has some MPs who have been accused of financial impropriety," said Labour's foreign affairs spokesman Robin Cook.
"But (it is) that the Tory leadership has consistently responded by protecting their party from being embarrassed rather than defending parliament from being corrupted."
A poll in Friday's Independent newspaper showed Labour's lead over the Conservatives, bidding for a record fifth successive term, grew to 27 points from 25 in the past week.
The election was announced on Monday, giving Britain its longest campaign for 80 years.

But Major, determined to extend the Conservatives' 18 years in power, found a glimmer of hope in the Harris poll which found most voters still believe Major could win even though the odds are currently stacked so highly against him.

The Guardian said Smith was appointed minister in January 1994 despite admitting to Major's parliamentary business manager four years earlier that he had been paid by Mohammed Al-Fayed, the Egyptian-born owner of London's upmarket store, Harrods.
Major was told of the allegations in September, it said.
Smith quit his post on October 20 saying he had been foolish and mistaken not to register the payments, but denying firmly that taking the money had been wrong or corrupt.
Major said Smith quit the day after he had received a report on the affair and called the Guardian's report "nonsense".
"It's total and complete junk. And what is more the Guardian should have known it," he said.
"As soon as the cabinet secretary reported, Mr Smith left the government the next day. It's not a fresh matter," said Major, on a campaign trip before returning to his constituency.
The latest twist in the row was fuelled by the Guardian's publication on Friday of extracts from secret evidence given to a parliamentary ethics watchdog after the start of the scandal.
This followed a furious row between Major and Labour leader Tony Blair in parliament on Thursday on the watchdog's inquiry.
An interim report by the watchdog, Sir Gordon Downey, parliament's commissioner for standards, on Thursday cleared 15 members of parliament of any wrongdoing.
But Downey said his report on Neil Hamilton, Smith and eight other Conservative MPs would not be ready until next week.
Major had ordered parliament's closure on Friday, launching a six-week campaign and effectively burying the report until after the election.
Downey has been looking into the alleged payments by Al-Fayed. He has also examined payments made as election expenses to several MPs by a parliamentary lobbyist, Ian Greer.

Labour broadened its attack on the Conservatives on Friday, calling for a probe into the ruling party's funding, kept secret by the Conservatives, and promising tougher rules of conduct for ministers.
